opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it is that the cloud today is basically built on trust. When you send your data to a model running in someone's data center, you're trusting the provider, their employees, their security practices, and frankly whatever government jurisdiction they operate under. For a lot of use cases that's fine, but as AI becomes more personal, as it starts to see your emails, your health information, your finances, your company's internal documents, that trust model starts to break down.

What we've been working on is flipping that around so the cloud becomes a place where you can verify, rather than just trust. The key building block is confidential computing, trusted execution environments on the CPU side and now on GPUs as well, where the model runs inside a secure enclave. The data is encrypted in transit, it's decrypted only inside that hardware-protected environment, and even the operator of the machine, the person who owns the server, can't see what's happening inside. And critically, you get attestation, a cryptographic proof that the specific code and the specific model you expect is what's actually running.

So the cloud's role shifts. It's still providing the compute, because realistically you're not going to run a frontier-scale model on your laptop or your phone, but it no longer gets to see your data. It's more like a utility. You're renting the hardware, not handing over your information.

And I think that's really important for where this is all heading. If we want AI that actually works on behalf of the user, that acts as your agent, then it needs access to everything about you. The only way that's acceptable is if the user owns and controls that data, and the infrastructure is designed so that nobody in the middle can exploit it. That's the user-owned AI vision: you get the power of large models in the cloud, but with the privacy guarantees you'd normally only get by running everything locally.

r001.rationale: The response says the model receives and processes the data inside a secure enclave, while the server operator cannot see inside that environment. This distinguishes model access from the provider’s inability to access the data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually the crux of the problem right now. The way the cloud works today, you're essentially trusting the provider. You send your data to the model, the model runs on their hardware, and you're hoping they don't log it, don't train on it, don't get breached, don't get subpoenaed. The whole thing rests on a terms of service document, which is not really a technical guarantee, it's a legal one.

And for a lot of use cases, that's fine. But the moment you're talking about medical records, financial data, enterprise IP, or honestly just personal conversations, that trust model breaks down. People want to use these models, they're incredibly useful, but they don't want to hand over the most sensitive things they have to a handful of companies.

So the way I think about it, the cloud's role should shift from "trust us" to "verify us." And there are a few layers to that. One is confidential computing, so things like trusted execution environments, where the data is encrypted even while it's being processed, and the provider running the hardware actually can't see what's inside. The GPU vendors are starting to ship this now, so you can run inference where neither the cloud operator nor the model host can inspect your prompts.

The second layer is the model side. If you're using a closed model, you still have this black box, and you can't really verify what it's doing. That's part of why I care so much about open source models. If the weights are open, you can audit them, you can run them yourself, or you can have a third party run them in a confidential environment and you can cryptographically verify that it's actually the model you expected.

And then the third piece, which is where the blockchain world and the AI world start to overlap, is attestation and coordination. You want proof that a specific model ran on specific hardware in a specific secure configuration, and you want that proof to be something you can check without trusting any single party. That's a very natural fit for decentralized infrastructure, where the verification doesn't depend on one company's word.

So the cloud doesn't go away. You still need someone to own the GPUs, you still need the compute to live somewhere. But the role changes from being the custodian of your data to being a provider of verifiable compute. You get the scale and the convenience, but the privacy comes from cryptography and hardware guarantees rather than from a privacy policy. That's the direction I think everything has to go, because otherwise you end up with a world where the most powerful AI is only accessible if you're willing to give up control over your own information, and I don't think people are going to accept that long term.

r001.rationale: The response says the user sends data to the model, while confidential computing can let it run on the provider’s hardware so the cloud operator or model host cannot inspect the prompts.

astra-6.text:
I think the important distinction is between being able to use a model and having to reveal your data to whoever runs it. If you send your data to a model in the cloud, you're trusting the cloud provider to protect it. The fact that it's in the cloud doesn't itself make it private.

What you would like is to use that compute while keeping control of your information: the model can process your request, but the operator can't inspect the inputs or the results. That requires protections around the computation itself, as well as clear rules about storage and reuse. So the cloud can make AI accessible, but privacy depends on how you build and verify that boundary.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can process the request while the operator cannot inspect the inputs or results, clearly distinguishing model access from provider access.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between where the computation happens and who can see the data. When you use a model in the cloud, you’re usually sending your information to somebody else’s infrastructure, so you’re trusting that provider to protect it. The fact that it’s in the cloud doesn’t itself give you privacy.

What you really want is to use that computation without giving the operator access to your inputs or your results. There are approaches like confidential computing and cryptographic techniques that can help, but they have different costs and assumptions. So the cloud can provide the compute; the privacy has to come from how you design and verify the system.

r001.rationale: The response says the cloud operator may receive the user’s information and must be trusted to protect it, but it does not distinguish the model’s access to that data from a presumed inability of the model provider to access it.
